400.title: Bezalel's hands (Exodus 35:30–35)
400.hook: the first person filled with the Spirit in the Bible is a craftsman
400.howItsDone: Many Christians see craft and good work as a way of honoring God, and churches have long blessed builders, artists and artisans; some congregations hold services blessing tools or the work of people's hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hesed, and God's name proclaimed right after the calf: merciful, gracious, long of nostrils. Your line was slow to anger. Did you catch one long breath before you spoke? Day four hundred.

Day four hundred. Quick question. In the Bible, who is the first person God is said to fill with his spirit? A prophet, you'd guess. A priest. Moses himself, maybe. Pharaoh once said the spirit of God was in Joseph, but the first time the text says God filled someone, it's none of those. It's a man named Bezalel. And what does the spirit fill him for? Not to preach. Not to perform miracles. To work with gold and silver and bronze, to cut stones and carve wood, and to make beautiful things. He's a craftsman. The tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among the people, needs building. And God picks the person who's good with his hands.
screen: `WHO WAS FILLED FIRST?` → `NOT A PROPHET. NOT A PRIEST.` → `A CRAFTSMAN.`

segments.voice: Moses tells the people, in the King James Bible, that God has called Bezalel by name, "And he hath filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Look at that list. Wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and then, without a pause, workmanship. The text puts skill with your hands in the same breath as wisdom. In this book, making something well is a spiritual gift. Bezalel isn't alone. He's given a partner, Oholiab, from another tribe, and the passage says God put it in his heart to teach. So the gift isn't hoarded. It's passed on, workshop style, to everyone the text calls wise-hearted: the women spinning blue and purple yarn, the men carving acacia wood, the jewelers setting stones. Whole sections of Exodus are spent on curtains and clasps, lampstands and loops, measured down to the cubit. People skip those chapters. But the Bible takes its time there, as if to say: this matters too. His name is lovely as well. Bezalel means, in the shadow of God. And notice the timing. This comes right after the golden calf. The people's gold went into an idol, and now gold, given freely, goes into a place for God to dwell. Same material, same hands, two different directions. Christians have taken this passage as a blessing on every kind of craft: the stonemasons of the great cathedrals, quilters and carpenters, the person who fixes your car well. In this story, the spirit of God fills a workshop before it fills a pulpit.
screen: `WISDOM, AND WORKMANSHIP.` · `PUT IN HIS HEART TO TEACH.` · `IN THE SHADOW OF GOD.` · `GOLD FOR A CALF, GOLD FOR A TENT.` · then, large: `FILLED WITH THE SPIRIT OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make something with care. It can be very small. Right after the bell, or while it rings if your hands are free: fold a cloth perfectly. Sharpen a pencil. Arrange three things on a table so they look right together. Wash one cup slowly, all the way around. Pay attention to the material in your hands: its weight, its texture, the way it answers you. Do it the way Bezalel might, as if the work itself were an offering. If you pray, you can offer it. The bell holds the time.
Bezalel's hands. The craftsman of the tabernacle, the first person the Bible says was filled with the spirit of God, for wisdom and for workmanship.
Your line: craft is spiritual. Today, take one ordinary task, a meal, an email, a repair, and do it as well as you can, slowly, on purpose. Day four hundred.

401.title: Love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:9–18)
401.hook: leave the edges of the field for the poor; love your neighbor as yourself
401.howItsDone: Christians learn 'love thy neighbour as thyself' as the second great commandment, and some churches and farms practice modern gleaning, gathering leftover crops after harvest for food banks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bezalel, the craftsman filled with the spirit of God. Your line was craft is spiritual. What did you do slowly and well? Day four hundred one.

Leviticus can be slow going: sacrifices, skin diseases, mildew, priestly clothing. And then, in the middle of it, chapter nineteen. A farmer is bringing in the harvest. The sickles swing through the wheat, row after row, and when they reach the corners of the field, they stop. On purpose. They leave the corners standing. Behind them, a few stalks have fallen to the ground, and nobody goes back to pick them up. In the vineyard, a few grapes have dropped, and they're left lying there too. It looks like sloppy farming. It's actually the law.
screen: `LEVITICUS: SLOW GOING?` → `THE SICKLES STOP AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE FALLEN STALKS STAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." And the grapes too: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the LORD your God." It's welfare built into the field itself. The poor don't have to beg at the farmhouse door. They walk into the field and gather what was left for them, with their own hands, with dignity. That's exactly how Ruth, a poor foreign widow, ends up gleaning in the field of Boaz, a story the path reaches next year. The Jewish oral law later gave a whole tractate of the Mishnah to these corners, called Peah, corner. Then chapter nineteen keeps going, line after line, all ordinary life. Don't hold back a worker's wages overnight. "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind." Don't spread gossip. Don't stand idle while your neighbor's life is in danger. Don't hate your brother in your heart. Don't take revenge or bear a grudge. And then, at the end of the list, almost tucked in: "but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." This is the line Jesus will quote as the second great commandment, straight from Leviticus. And look at the shape of the chapter. Love your neighbor isn't a warm feeling floating in the air. It's corners of fields, wages paid on time, the deaf and the blind protected, grudges dropped. Love has edges you can see. And later in the same chapter, the law says the stranger among you is to be loved as yourself too.
screen: `DON'T REAP THE CORNERS.` · `THE POOR GLEAN WITH DIGNITY.` · `NO GRUDGES, NO STUMBLING BLOCKS.` · `THE LINE JESUS WILL QUOTE.` · then, large: `“THOU SHALT LOVE THY NEIGHBOUR AS THYSELF.”`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something for others. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own field: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, your parking spot, the last slice, the best seat. Where are the corners? Where could you stop the sickle a little early and leave something standing, without making a speech about it? Maybe a few dollars where someone will find them. The good parking space. An hour of your week. Choose one corner. Picture someone else gathering it. If you pray, you can pray for whoever will. The bell holds the time.
Peah. Hebrew for corner, the Mishnah's name for the harvest law: leaving the edges of the field standing for the poor and the stranger.
Your line: leave the edges. Today, don't take all of something: leave the last of it, quietly, for someone else to find. Day four hundred one.

402.title: Jubilee (Leviticus 25:8–12)
402.hook: every fiftieth year, debts forgiven, land returned, liberty proclaimed
402.howItsDone: Christians hear the jubilee in Jesus' reading at Nazareth, the Catholic Church declares holy years called jubilees, and some churches have used the idea to campaign for debt relief for poor countries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peah: the corners of the field left standing for the poor, and love your neighbor as yourself. Your line was leave the edges. What did you leave for someone else? Day four hundred two.

In Philadelphia there's a bell with a crack running up its side. Visitors line up to see it. Around the top, cast into the metal, is a line of scripture, with the reference right there: Leviticus, chapter twenty-five, verse ten. It's easy to read the words and think of the American Revolution. Abolitionists later took the bell as their symbol and gave it the name it still has, the Liberty Bell. But the words on it are far older, and about something stranger and more radical than independence. A year when everything, in a sense, resets.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `LEVITICUS 25:10, CAST IN METAL.` → `A YEAR WHEN EVERYTHING RESETS.`

segments.voice: The law counts in sevens. Every seventh day, rest. Every seventh year, the land rests too. Then count seven sevens of years, forty-nine, and on the Day of Atonement a ram's horn sounds through the whole land. Here's the verse on the bell, in the King James Bible: "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family." In that fiftieth year, land that had been sold goes back to the family it was first given to. People who had sold themselves into service because of debt go free and go home. The reason is given a few verses later: the land is mine, God says, and you're strangers and sojourners with me. Nobody owns anything forever. The Hebrew name for the year is yovel, a word for a ram's horn, and English jubilee comes from it. Did Israel ever actually keep it? The Bible gives the law, but it never describes a jubilee year being kept. Nobody can say for sure. But the idea never went away. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus stands up in the synagogue at Nazareth and reads from Isaiah, about liberty for captives and the acceptable year of the Lord, and some readers hear the jubilee ringing in it. The Catholic Church still declares holy years called jubilees. And a church-backed campaign took the name Jubilee to press rich nations to cancel the debts of poor countries.
screen: `SEVEN SEVENS, THEN A HORN.` · `LAND RETURNED, PEOPLE GO HOME.` · `THE LAND IS MINE.` · `DID THEY KEEP IT? NOBODY'S SURE.` · then, large: `PROCLAIM LIBERTY THROUGHOUT ALL THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive a small debt. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone owes you. Maybe money: ten dollars, a lunch, a loan you've stopped expecting. Maybe something else: an apology, a favor returned, a phone call. Notice how often you've mentally added it up. Now picture the ram's horn sounding. Picture letting it go home. Not because it didn't matter, but because you'd rather be free of carrying it. If it's money and you can, decide to tell them it's forgiven. If you pray, you can hand the ledger to God. The bell holds the time.
Jubilee. From the Hebrew yovel, a ram's horn. Every fiftieth year in the law, land returned and people freed, liberty proclaimed through the land.
Your line: proclaim liberty. Today, cancel one small debt, out loud if you can: you don't owe me that anymore. Day four hundred two.

403.title: The priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
403.hook: the Lord bless you and keep you, make his face shine on you
403.carry: the lord bless you and keep you
403.howItsDone: Some pastors and priests say the Aaronic blessing at the end of worship with raised hands, and it is spoken at some weddings, baptisms and funerals; in synagogues, kohanim may say it over the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jubilee: a ram's horn, land returned, people sent home free. Your line was proclaim liberty. Did you cancel a small debt? Day four hundred three.

In burial caves just outside Jerusalem, archaeologists once found two tiny rolled-up scrolls of silver, each small enough to hide in your palm. They were so fragile that unrolling them took great care. When they were finally opened, scratched into the silver were a few lines of Hebrew. Someone had worn them, perhaps as amulets, maybe around the neck. And the words inside were a blessing, the same blessing churches and synagogues still speak today. Three lines that people have been carrying close ever since.
screen: `TWO SILVER SCROLLS IN A TOMB.` → `SMALL ENOUGH TO WEAR.` → `THE WORDS INSIDE: A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: In the book of Numbers, God tells Moses to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests: this is how you shall bless the people. And then the words, in the King James Bible: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Three lines. And they grow. In Hebrew, the first line is three words, the second five, the third seven. Like a wave building. Each line names the LORD, and then gives two gifts. Bless and keep: provide for you and guard you. Shine and be gracious: the picture is a face lighting up when it sees you, the way a grandparent's face does when you walk in. Lift up his countenance: turn toward you, look right at you. And the last word, the one everything has been building to, is shalom: peace, wholeness, nothing missing. Notice too that it's thee, singular. In Hebrew, the blessing is spoken to the whole people, but every you is a single you. A crowd is blessed, one person at a time. Then God says why: "they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The priests speak the words. God does the blessing. In synagogues it can be said by the kohanim, families who trace their line to the priests. Churches use it too: some ministers and priests raise their hands and say it at the end of a service, at a wedding, over a newborn, at a grave.
screen: `THREE LINES: THREE, FIVE, SEVEN WORDS.` · `A FACE THAT LIGHTS UP.` · `ENDING IN SHALOM.` · `PRIESTS SPEAK, GOD BLESSES.` · then, large: `THE LORD MAKE HIS FACE SHINE UPON THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the blessing over someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person: someone you love, someone you're worried about, or someone you find difficult. See their face. Then, quietly, aloud or inside, say the old words over them, slowly, one line per breath. The LORD bless thee, and keep thee. The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace. If those words aren't yours to say, simply hold them in mind and wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Shalom. Hebrew for peace, wholeness, nothing missing: the last word of the priestly blessing, building like a wave from bless to peace.
Your line: the lord bless you and keep you. Today, say it, or think it, over one person as they leave the room. Day four hundred three.

404.title: Twelve spies (Numbers 13–14)
404.hook: ten see giants and feel like grasshoppers; two see a good land
404.howItsDone: Christians tell the story of the twelve spies to talk about courage and trust in God, and Caleb is held up in sermons and youth programs as a model of wholehearted faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shalom: three lines growing toward peace. Your line was the lord bless you and keep you. Who did you say it over? Day four hundred four.
screen: `THE LORD BLESS YOU AND KEEP YOU.`

segments.voice: Twelve men come back from a forty-day scouting trip. Two of them are carrying a pole between them on their shoulders, and hanging from the pole is a single cluster of grapes. One bunch, and it takes a pole and two men. The whole camp crowds around. The land is real, and it's rich. It flows with milk and honey, the scouts say. And then most of them keep talking. But. The cities are walled and huge. The people are strong. And there are giants. We saw them. Next to them, we looked like grasshoppers. Two of the twelve look at the same grapes, the same walls, the same giants, and tell a completely different story.
screen: `ONE CLUSTER, TWO MEN, ONE POLE.` → `MILK AND HONEY. BUT.` → `WE LOOKED LIKE GRASSHOPPERS.`

segments.voice: Here's how the ten put it, in the King James Bible: "we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight." Read that slowly. First, in our own sight. Then, and so we were in their sight. They decided how small they were before anyone else did. And they never actually asked the giants. Caleb, one of the two, quiets the crowd and says: "Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it." Joshua stands with him. Same facts. Different eyes. The ten saw the walls and measured them against themselves. Caleb and Joshua saw the walls and measured them against God, who had opened a sea for them. But the crowd believes the ten. That night they weep. Let's choose a captain and go back to Egypt, they say. They even talk about stoning Caleb and Joshua. And the consequence is heavy: forty years in the wilderness, a year for every day the spies were gone, until that generation has passed. Their children will enter the land they were afraid of. Of all those counted from twenty years old and up, only Caleb and Joshua will walk in. God says of Caleb that he "had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully." Caleb is the quiet hero of this story, and the Bible comes back to him. Forty-five years later, in the book of Joshua, he's eighty-five, still strong, and he asks for the hill country where the giants lived. Today Israel's Ministry of Tourism uses two men carrying the grapes on a pole as its emblem.
screen: `A CLUSTER, AND A BUT.` · `IN OUR OWN SIGHT, GRASSHOPPERS.` · `WE ARE WELL ABLE.` · `FORTY YEARS, A YEAR FOR A DAY.` · then, large: `HE HAD ANOTHER SPIRIT, AND FOLLOWED ME FULLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one challenge Caleb's way. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in front of you that feels like a walled city. A hard conversation. An exam. A diagnosis. A job you're not sure you can do. Notice the grasshopper voice: who you think you are next to it. Now look again with Caleb's eyes. Same walls. But what have you already come through? Who's with you? What grapes are hanging from this, what good is on the other side? If you pray, you can measure it against God instead of yourself. The bell holds the time.
Twelve spies. Sent to scout the land: ten came back feeling like grasshoppers, and two, Caleb and Joshua, said, we are well able.
Your line: we're not grasshoppers. Today, when you hear yourself shrink in front of something big, say it under your breath, and take one step toward it. Day four hundred four.

405.title: Balaam's donkey (Numbers 22:21–35)
405.hook: a donkey sees the angel her master can't, and speaks
405.howItsDone: Christians often tell Balaam's story to children for its humor and to adults as a reminder that God can speak through unlikely voices; the New Testament mentions Balaam and his donkey in 2 Peter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve spies, a cluster of grapes on a pole, and Caleb saying we are well able. Your line was we're not grasshoppers. What did you step toward? Day four hundred five.

A king named Balak is frightened. A huge people has camped on his border, the Israelites, fresh from the desert. So he sends for a famous seer named Balaam, a man known for blessings and curses that stick. Come and curse this people for me, he says, and I'll pay you well. Balaam saddles his donkey and sets out. And this is where the Bible tells one of its funniest, strangest stories. On the road, the donkey suddenly swerves into a field. Balaam beats her back onto the road. Then she squeezes against a wall and crushes his foot. He beats her again. Then she just lies down under him. And Balaam, furious, beats her a third time.
screen: `A KING HIRES A CURSE.` → `THE DONKEY SWERVES, SQUEEZES, LIES DOWN.` → `THREE BEATINGS.`

segments.voice: Then this, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?" And here's the funny part: Balaam argues back. He doesn't seem surprised that his donkey is talking. You've made a fool of me, he says. If I had a sword I'd kill you. And she answers, reasonably: haven't I carried you all your life? Have I ever done this before? And he has to admit, no. "Then the LORD opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand." The donkey had seen it all along, three times. The famous seer, the professional who sees what others can't, is the only one on the road who's blind. And his donkey saved his life. The angel says so: if she hadn't turned aside, I would have killed you and let her live. The rest of the story is just as surprising. Balaam goes on to King Balak, climbs the hills three times to curse Israel, and three times blessing comes out of his mouth instead. One of those blessings, how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, is still said in Jewish morning prayers. And in 1967, archaeologists in Jordan found a plaster inscription from around the eighth century before Christ that names Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods. He was remembered outside the Bible too. The lesson Christians have long drawn: God can speak through anyone. Even a donkey.
screen: `WHAT HAVE I DONE UNTO THEE?` · `THE SEER IS THE ONE WHO'S BLIND.` · `THE CURSE COMES OUT A BLESSING.` · `HIS NAME ON A WALL IN JORDAN.` · then, large: `THE LORD OPENED THE MOUTH OF THE ASS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an unlikely messenger. Settle, and breathe. Think of the voices in your life you tend to brush off. A child who says something too blunt. A coworker you don't respect much. A critic. A stranger. Your own tired body, lying down under you in the road. Has one of them been trying to tell you something, maybe more than once? Picture yourself stopping, getting off the donkey, and actually listening. If you pray, you can ask to have your eyes opened like Balaam's. The bell holds the time.
Balaam's donkey. She saw the angel in the road three times, while her famous master saw nothing, and then she spoke.
Your line: even a donkey can see. Today, take one piece of advice seriously from someone you'd normally ignore. Day four hundred five.

406.title: Slavery in the law, honestly
406.hook: the books that say love your neighbor also regulate slavery; some laws limit it, some are hard to read, and Christians read them in different ways
406.howItsDone: Christians read the Old Testament's slavery laws in different ways: as limits on an ancient practice, as concessions to hardness of heart, or as human words of their time. Churches today teach that slavery is a grave wrong, and many point to the image of God in every person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Balaam's donkey, who saw the angel her master couldn't. Your line was even a donkey can see. Today, something many readers would rather not see: some of the hardest pages in the law. Day four hundred six.

A teenager posts a question online: why does the Bible allow slavery? The replies pile up. Some explain it away. Some defend it. The reply with the most votes says only that it's disturbing to watch people justify it. And the question itself barely gets answered. So here it is, straight. The laws of Moses, the same books that say love your neighbor as yourself and proclaim liberty in the jubilee, also regulate slavery. Today's word is the Hebrew for servant, or slave.
screen: `WHY DOES THE BIBLE ALLOW SLAVERY?` → `EXPLAINED AWAY, OR DEFENDED.` → `SO HERE IT IS, STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Ebed. In Hebrew it can mean servant, worker or slave, and the context decides. Moses himself is called the ebed of the LORD. But in these laws it often means a person owned by another. Some of the laws limit it. In the King James Bible: "If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free." He's to be sent off with gifts, and the reason is given: "thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." Another law forbids handing an escaped slave back to his master. Kidnapping a person to sell carried the death penalty. Other laws are hard to read. Foreigners could be bought, and "they shall be your bondmen for ever." A master who beats a slave who survives a day or two goes unpunished, "for he is his money." Honest readers don't pretend that's gentle. So how do Christians read these pages? Some point to the ancient world, where slavery was everywhere, and see these laws as limits on it, a first step. Some point to Jesus, who said Moses allowed divorce "because of the hardness of your hearts," and read the slavery laws the same way: allowed, not blessed. Some say plainly that these laws reflect their writers' world, not God's will for any time. Jewish readers have their own long tradition of wrestling with them too. And in nineteenth-century America, both sides quoted the Bible. Defenders of slavery quoted these laws and Paul. Abolitionists quoted the kidnapping law, the image of God in every person, and Paul's "neither bond nor free." The same law that regulates the ebed begins with slaves in Egypt crying out, and being heard.
screen: `EBED: SERVANT, OR SLAVE.` · `IN THE SEVENTH HE SHALL GO OUT FREE.` · `FOR HE IS HIS MONEY.` · `BOTH SIDES QUOTED THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't defend it, don't skip it. Settle, and breathe. Let one of today's hard lines sit in front of you: for he is his money. Don't explain it. Just let it be as hard as it is. Then bring to mind the people, in the ancient world and in later centuries, who lived under words like these. Hold them for a moment with respect. If you pray, you can bring the hard verse to God as it is, the way Israel cried out in Egypt. If you don't, simply stay honest with it. The bell holds the time.
Ebed. Hebrew for servant, or slave: the word in the laws that limit slavery, and in the laws that are hard to read.
Your line: read the hard parts honestly. No defending, no skipping. Day four hundred six.

fork.setup: a friend reads Exodus 21 for the first time and says: this is awful. what do you do?
options: explain why it's actually fine.
agree it's hard, and share how different readers wrestle with it.
tell them to skip that part.
fork.reveal: honest readers say it plainly: "for he is his money" is hard to read. then they show how they wrestle with it, without defending it or skipping it.

original.note: Hebrew: servant, worker or slave. Moses is called the ebed of the LORD (Deuteronomy 34:5).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible either clearly approves of slavery, or never mentions it.
what it means: the law regulates slavery. some laws limit it, some are hard to read, and Christians read them in different ways.

what a scholar hears: Hebrew ebed covers servant, vassal and slave; the Torah treats Hebrew debt-servants (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15) differently from foreign slaves (Leviticus 25:44–46), and Deuteronomy 23:15–16 forbids returning a runaway.
